# Exponential tilt, reciprocal convexity, and tilted opposite-pair variance

Let (Y_1,\ldots,Y_N) be independent unit-rate exponential random
variables. Fix a real vector (c) with at least one positive and at least
one negative coordinate, and put

    V=sum_i c_i Y_i,  f=f_V,  F=Pr(V>=0),
    mu_i=E(Y_i | V=0).

Conditioning means the actual coarea conditional measure at zero.
The density (f) is continuous and strictly positive at zero; the section
means are finite and positive. Zero coordinates are permitted and have
mean one. The statements below concern ordinary simplex-section data;
they do not prove a general mixed-integer depth bound.

## 1. The exact tilt orbit

Write (p=\max_{c_i>0}c_i), (r=\max_{c_i<0}|c_i|), and

    I=(-1/r,1/p), beta_i(t)=1-t c_i,
    Z(t)=product_i beta_i(t), c_i(t)=c_i/beta_i(t).

Every beta is positive on I. Exponential tilting of the joint law by

    Z(t) exp(t V)

produces independent exponential coordinates of rates beta_i. After the
coordinate change (Y'_i=\beta_iY_i), the new coordinates are again
independent unit-rate exponentials and their linear form is

    sum_i c_i(t)Y'_i=V.

The tilt factor is constant on the section V=0. Thus the original
conditional law of Y there is unchanged, and the new conditional means
and linear-form density satisfy exactly

    mu_i(t)=beta_i(t) mu_i,
    f_t(v)=Z(t) exp(tv) f(v).                         (1)

These identities follow either directly from coarea, whose same linear
form is retained before rescaling, or by disintegrating the tilted joint
density. In particular no approximation of a conditioning event of
probability zero is being substituted for the section law.

Define the positive and negative half-transforms

    A(t)=integral_0^infinity exp(tv) f(v) dv,
    B(t)=integral_-infinity^0 exp(tv) f(v) dv.

All their derivatives exist on I by exponential domination on compact
subintervals. They obey

    A(t)+B(t)=1/Z(t),  F_t=Z(t)A(t),
    G(t):=F_t(1-F_t)/Z(t)=A(t)B(t)/(A(t)+B(t)),
    H(t):=1/G(t)=1/A(t)+1/B(t).                      (2)

For every omitted index j, equation (1) gives the exact quotient relation

    product_(i!=j)mu_i(t) / [F_t(1-F_t)]
      = product_(i!=j)mu_i / [beta_j(t)G(t)].        (3)

For the full product the corresponding denominator is simply G(t).

## 2. Reciprocal convexity

We first record an elementary moment consequence of log-concavity.
If X has a log-concave density on [0,infinity), then

    Var(X)<=(EX)^2.                                (4)

Here is a proof with the relevant boundary conventions. Let g be its
density and S its survival function, normalized by S(0)=1. On the
interior of the positive-density interval, log-concavity implies that
g(x+u)/g(x) is nonincreasing in x for every u>=0. Integrating in u shows
that S(x)/g(x) is nonincreasing, so the hazard g/S is nondecreasing.
Consequently log S is concave wherever S>0, with the same conclusion by
continuity at its endpoints. If the support begins above zero, S=1
before that endpoint and the same hazard argument still applies.
The concavity of log S and log S(0)=0 imply

    S(a+b)<=S(a)S(b),  a,b>=0.

For example, this last inequality follows by integrating the
nonincreasing derivative of log S on [a,a+b] and [0,b]; approximation
handles nondifferentiability. Tonelli now gives

    EX^2/2=integral_0^infinity integral_0^infinity
                  S(a+b) da db <=(EX)^2,

which is (4). The conclusion also follows by truncation if a moment is
initially allowed to be infinite; all applications here have exponential
tails and finite moments.

The density f is log-concave: each nonzero c_iY_i has a log-concave
one-sided exponential density, and convolution preserves log-concavity
by the standard Prekopa theorem. Zero-coefficient variables can be
deleted. Restriction to either half-line and multiplication by exp(tv)
preserve log-concavity. Apply (4) to the positive-half tilted probability
density exp(tv)f(v)/A(t). Direct differentiation yields

    (1/A)''=(2A'^2-AA'')/A^3
            =[(E_t V)^2-Var_t(V)]/A >=0.

Applying the same argument to -V on the negative half-line gives
(1/B)''>=0. Hence

    H=1/G is convex on I.                          (5)

This statement is not convexity or concavity of G itself.

For a selected largest positive coefficient p, the reciprocal of
beta_p(t)G(t) is H(t)/(1-pt). Its derivative has numerator

    N(t)=(1-pt)H'(t)+pH(t),
    N'(t)=(1-pt)H''(t)>=0.                         (6)

Thus beta_p G increases and then decreases, with possible flat pieces
and with an endpoint supremum allowed. No strict uniqueness or interior
attainment is asserted. Formula (6) reduces optimization on one actual
tilt orbit to a single monotone derivative sign.

## 3. An exact selected-coordinate endpoint identity

For any positive coefficient c_j=p, not necessarily the largest, the
negative half-transform is finite at t=1/p and

    mu_j=B(1/p)/(p f(0)).                          (7)

To prove this without derivatives at a density seam, put
W=sum_(i!=j)c_iY_i and let nu be its probability law. Conditioning on W
gives

    f(v)=(1/p) integral_(w<=v) exp(-(v-w)/p) dnu(w).

Tonelli on v<0 implies

    B(1/p)=(1/p) integral_(w<0)(-w)exp(w/p)dnu(w).

On the section V=0, the forced value of Y_j is -w/p. Its first-moment
coarea integral is therefore

    f(0)mu_j=(1/p^2)integral_(w<0)(-w)exp(w/p)dnu(w),

which proves (7). The integrals are finite since (-w)exp(w/p) is bounded
on w<=0. This argument remains valid if W has an atom; in our mixed-sign
setting the displayed coarea integral is positive.

The same formula also proves that exp(v/p)f(v) is nondecreasing in v.
Neither this monotonicity nor (7) alone proves a variance-product bound.

## 4. Every tilt of an opposite-paired pattern pays the full product

Suppose the nonzero original coefficients occur in opposite pairs

    p_1,-p_1,...,p_k,-p_k,  p_i>0.

The proved theorem in
`candidate 135c08810eff7d45`
gives

    product_i mu_i>=1/4,

strictly if k>=2. Its elementary proof uses equal means within each
pair, each at most one, and total deficit one half among the k distinct
pair means. The base density f is even, so A(-t)=B(t), H is even, and
the tilt interval is symmetric. By convexity (5),

    H(t)>=H(0)=4,  G(t)<=1/4.

Multiplying the original full-product inequality by Z(t)>0 and using
(1)--(2) proves for every admissible finite tilt

    product_i mu_i(t)>=Z(t)/4
                     >=Z(t)G(t)=F_t(1-F_t).       (8)

It is strict whenever k>=2. Zero phases remain independent, with mean
one, and can be appended without changing (8). If a particular new mean
mu_j(t)<=1, removing it from the product preserves (8). No such
omitted-coordinate conclusion is inferred here when mu_j(t)>1.

There is a precise coefficient-only description of this family.
Given positive coefficients P_i paired with negative magnitudes R_i,
they arise by a common tilt from an opposite-paired pattern if and only
if all reciprocal differences 1/P_i-1/R_i are the same number -2t.
Indeed the forward formulas are

    P_i=p_i/(1-tp_i), R_i=p_i/(1+tp_i),
    p_i=2/(1/P_i+1/R_i).

These identities also verify the signs and admissibility of the recovered
tilt. Thus (8) is a full-product theorem for an explicitly described
asymmetric family with arbitrarily many phases. It is not a theorem for
every two-positive or every unpaired pattern.

## 5. The larger-positive theorem along an orbit, and a failed shortcut

For exactly two positive phases and any number of negative or zero
phases, let p be the larger positive coefficient. The proved result
`candidate fdab4307532951f8`
applies at every t in I: signs and the order of the positive coefficients
are preserved by c -> c/(1-tc). Equations (1)--(3) consequently imply

    product_(i!=p)mu_i >= sup_(t in I) beta_p(t)G(t),
    product_i mu_i >= mu_p sup_(t in I) beta_p(t)G(t).       (9)

An additional inequality

    mu_p sup_(t in I) beta_p(t)G(t) >= G(0)          (10)

would prove the full-product bound for this entire class. Inequality
(10) is a remaining functional claim, not a consequence established in
this note.

In particular the shortcut of choosing the tilt for which mu_p(t)=1
and assuming G(t)>=G(0) is false. Take actual coefficients

    c=(1,2,-2,-1).

The density is

    f(v)=[2exp(-|v|/2)-exp(-|v|)]/6.

Its section means are (5/6,2/3,2/3,5/6), and F=1/2. At t=-1/4,

    beta=(5/4,3/2,1/2,3/4), Z=45/64,
    c(t)=(4/5,4/3,-4,-4/3), F_t=7/32,
    beta_p mu_p=1,
    G(t)=35/144<1/4=G(0).                          (11)

All values follow by integrating the displayed two-exponential density.
This falsifies only that prescribed-tilt shortcut, not the supremum
inequality (10). The paired-tilt theorem (8) still proves the desired
full-product variance bound for every member of this example's orbit.
